abstract: Many organisms responsible for globally important processes, from carbon cycling to human disease, are microscopic eukaryotes. While their reproduction is essential for their success, across the tree of life, our understanding of evolutionary processes is limited due to the inherent challenges of studying microorganisms. Tools and predictions developed in multicellular and obligately sexual taxa are often not tractable in microbes, where population sizes can be large and extracting DNA from individuals is difficult. Even when sexual characteristics can be observed, population genetics is the only method available to characterize the reproductive mode. The relative rates of sexual versus clonal reproduction partition genetic diversity and are therefore integral to our understanding of evolutionary processes. We developed a single-cell population genetic approach to characterize the reproductive mode of the snow alga Chlainomonas sp. This Chlorophyte alga exhibits a complex life cycle, whereby bloom dynamics are directly observable in natural populations. We explored genetic diversity using single cells collected across several years of Chlainomonas sp. summer blooms. Dominant red cells in the bloom were diploid. Yet, all were unique genotypes, despite the prediction that clonal processes drive bloom development. We found high selfing rates, but selfing and clonality are often indistinguishable without understanding an organisms's natural history. Chlainomonas sp. has a haploid-diploid life cycle as hypothesized, engaging in both clonal and sexual reproduction, likely selfing. This study represents a first use of single cell population genetic methods to understand natural populations of partially clonal microeukaryotes.
